title: When Fear Of Noise Beats The Better Plan
documentTitle: In re Google Play Store Antitrust Litigation (Epic v. Google) — Exhibit 8526
excerptForBlog:
Policy change goals are to improve payment UX and ensure ecosystem consistency. Even though we have a defensible plan that achieves goals and made progress with many developers impacted, the sense is we'll likely not want to trigger Spotify agitation and associated noise with a policy change. I.e. the risk of likely Spotify agitation may be higher than the (harder to gauge) risk of status quo.

Option Summary:

• Remove Exception – Require exclusive Google Play Billing integration for all digital IAPs; provide generous grandfathering (2 yrs; minimal reqs). Advantage: removes policy ambiguity, improves payment UX, better positions Google to respond to regulatory inquiry. Key Risk: triggers Spotify agitation (high likelihood) and associated noise.

• Keep Exception; Add Requirements. Advantage: partially achieves improved payment UX; new requirements are defensible. Key Risk: draws attention to ambiguous exception, which may prove hard to justify → contagion.

• No Policy Change. Advantage: Google doesn't trigger noise. Key Risk: Regulator may deem exclusive Google Play Billing requirement unnecessary, partly due to current exception; more apps de-integrate Google Play Billing.

Question raised: Is it worth one more chat with Spotify to better assess how displeased they'd be if we changed policy, but provided generous grandfathering (e.g. 2 years and no requirements)? We owe them a response on their grandfathering counterproposal anyhow.

sourceCase: In re Google Play Store Antitrust Litigation (Epic v. Google)
lessonTitle: When Fear Of Noise Beats The Better Plan
situation: In December 2023, Google employees Kirsten Rasanen and Samer Sayigh circulated an internal options memo weighing whether to tighten Play Store billing policy — specifically, whether to require Google Play Billing for all digital in-app purchases. They lay out three paths and admit the team has 'a defensible plan' but will 'likely not want to trigger Spotify agitation and associated noise.'
insight:
The memo shows a leadership team quietly letting one powerful counterparty veto a policy they believe is right. The authors explicitly frame it as a **risk comparison**: known noise from Spotify versus the 'harder to gauge' risk of the status quo. Loud, near-term political cost is being weighted heavier than diffuse, longer-term regulatory cost — even as they name that regulators may later deem their billing requirement unnecessary precisely because of the exception they're afraid to close.

This is a classic **squeaky-wheel problem**. One vocal partner distorts platform-wide policy. Notice the tell: the third option, 'No Policy Change,' has an advantage listed only as avoiding noise — not as being substantively better. That's a team talking itself into inaction while documenting, in writing, that inaction is the weakest choice on the merits.
application: When you face a policy or pricing change, list the options like this memo does — but force yourself to write a *substantive* advantage for the status quo, not just 'avoids conflict.' If you can't, you've found your answer. Then ask: what's the smallest concession (here, 'generous grandfathering — 2 years') that lets you do the right thing while softening the loudest objector?
pullQuote: The best-designed policy loses to the loudest possible critic — until you honestly weigh the cost of doing nothing.
